There are no slides for this lecture. The page is built from the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Sultan's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no PAD chapter.

1. Atherosclerosis — pathophysiology

  • Atherosclerosis = a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium-sized arteries → plaque → narrowing/occlusion → reduced flow. Small-vessel disease is classified separately (microangiopathy).
  • Plaque cascade: (1) endothelial injury (chemical/mechanical) → inflammation, lipid and WBCs gather beneath the endothelium → (2) macrophages engulf lipid → foam cells → fatty streak → (3) fibrous plaque (inflammatory cells, smooth muscle, fibroblasts, calcium) → (4) progressive stenosis → (5) plaque rupture & thrombosis (platelet adhesion → occlusion).
  • Antiplatelets act only at step 5 — they prevent platelet thrombosis but don't treat the plaque itself.
Non-modifiableModifiable — MAJOR (memorize)Modifiable — additional
Increasing ageDiabetes mellitusObesity
Male sexSmokingPhysical inactivity
Family history / geneticsHypertensionInsulin resistance
Dyslipidaemia
  • The most important modifiable major risk factor among the options → diabetes mellitus (obesity is minor; family history and male sex aren't modifiable). 438

2. PAD — significance & prognosis

  • PAD = atherosclerotic obstruction of the lower-limb arterial circulation, including the aorta and its distal branches.
  • PAD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis — associated with coronary and cerebrovascular disease, MI, stroke and increased mortality. MI is the more frequent event; cardiovascular events and death are commoner than amputation. Leg pulses are a window onto arterial disease that coronaries can't give.
  • Most PAD is asymptomatic → finding it allows early, aggressive risk reduction. Greater severity → higher CV morbidity and mortality.
  • Mortality (lecture): ~25% at 5 years · ~50% at 10 · ~75% at 15 · 6–7% per year. A PAD patient is more likely to die of an MI or stroke than to lose the leg.

3. Clinical presentation

  • Spectrum: asymptomatic (the majority) → intermittent claudication → CLTI: ischaemic rest pain → ulceration/tissue loss → gangrene.
  • No claudication ≠ no PAD — limited activity can hide ischaemia.

Intermittent claudication

  • Reproducible, exercise-induced muscle pain from insufficient arterial supply, relieved by rest. It arises in the muscles fed by the diseased artery, so its site localizes the lesion. Claudication distance shrinks as disease progresses (1 km → 500 m → 200 m).
Level of diseaseClaudication siteWhy
Aortoiliac / common iliacButtock / glutealLesion above the internal iliac origin → gluteal muscles under-perfused
External iliac / proximal femoralThighInternal iliac intact → gluteal perfusion preserved
More distal (SFA, popliteal, tibial)CalfOnly the distal muscles are ischaemic
Vascular claudicationNeurogenic claudication
CauseInsufficient arterial supply to exercising muscleNeural compression (spinal stenosis)
PatternReproducible exertional painOften posture-dependent
ReliefStopping/rest — no change of position neededMay need sitting or spinal flexion
  • Diabetic, leg pain and numbness after 500 m, must stop and rest to relieve it, normal neuro exam → vascular claudication. 438
Added explanationLeriche syndrome (aortoiliac occlusion) = buttock/thigh claudication + absent femoral pulses + erectile dysfunction (impotence).
  • Leriche syndrome — absent femoral pulses + bilateral claudication + impotence. 438 ×2
Added explanationCalf claudication in a young non-smoker → think popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (the artery is compressed by the medial head of gastrocnemius) — atherosclerosis and Buerger's disease need risk factors (age, smoking).
  • Most common cause of calf claudication in a 20-year-old non-smoker → popliteal entrapment syndrome. 427 ×2

Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI)

  • CLTI = advanced PAD with ischaemic rest pain and/or tissue loss (ulcer or gangrene). Assess symptoms, walking distance, rest pain, tissue loss and overall severity.

4. Physical examination

  • Examine the lower-limb pulses and look for chronic ischaemia: dry skin, nail changes, loss of hair, poor tissue quality, muscle wasting, ulceration, tissue loss, gangrene.
SignWhat you seeMeaning
Elevation pallorFoot turns pale when raisedInadequate arterial perfusion
Dependent ruborFoot turns red when loweredDilated ischaemic vessels + dependent filling
UlcerTissue defect with a visible base; may expose boneTissue loss from chronic ischaemia
GangreneTissue necrosisAdvanced ischaemia
  • "Pale when up, red when down."
Added explanationIschaemic ulcers are on the toes/between the toes, heel and pressure points — painful, punched-out, pale base with poor granulation, cold pulseless foot. Venous ulcers are at the medial malleolus (gaiter area); neuropathic ulcers are painless, under the metatarsal heads.
  • Sign supporting a non-healing ischaemic ulcer → between the 1st and 2nd toes, tender, with poor granulation tissue. 437 ×2

5. Investigations

  • Objectives: (1) diagnose and grade PAD · (2) assess systemic risk (lipids, glucose, BP) · (3) define anatomy only if intervention is considered.

Ankle–brachial index (ABI)

  • ABI = higher ankle systolic pressure (DP or PT) ÷ higher brachial systolic pressure (either arm), for each leg — 6 readings (2 arms + DP and PT on each side). Use the higher brachial for both legs (avoids error from a unilateral arm stenosis).
  • Worked example: brachial 100 and 120 → denominator 120. Ankle 120 and 100 → ABI = 120/120 = 1.0; ankle 50 and 60 → 60/120 = 0.5.
ABIMeaning
> 1.40Non-compressible (calcified) arteries — falsely high, not excellent perfusion (values of ~1.5, even ~2)
1.00 – 1.40Normal
0.91 – 0.99Borderline
≤ 0.90PAD — the lower, the more severe and the worse the cardiovascular risk
  • Falsely high ABI (diabetes, CKD, calcified vessels) → use toe pressure / toe–brachial index (digital arteries calcify less). Lecture value: toe systolic ≥ 70 mmHg ≈ normal.
  • How to calculate the ABI → ankle systolic BP / brachial systolic BP. 439
  • ABI 1.0 → normal. 439 ×2
  • Calf claudication at 500 m, palpable femoral pulse, absent pulses below → next vascular test ankle–brachial index. 438 ×5

Imaging

Duplex USCT angiographyMR angiographyCatheter angiography
ShowsStructure + flow velocity/waveformsDetailed anatomy, 3DArterial anatomyStenosis/occlusion, distal flow
Radiation/contrastNeitherRadiation + IV contrastNo ionizing radiationInvasive arterial access
PracticalitiesCheap, painlessFast (~5 min), less operator-dependentExpensive, slow, motion-sensitiveProcedure-based
LimitationOperator-dependentContrast and radiationLess practical in someInvasive
Best useUncertain findings; characterize diseasePlanning revascularizationImaging without radiationWhen an endovascular procedure is planned
  • Doppler: a stenosis → ↑ local velocity and abnormal downstream waveforms. Routine anatomical imaging is not needed for every stable PAD patient.
  • Anatomy: aorta → common iliac → internal iliac (pelvis, gluteal, penile) + external iliac → common femoral (under the inguinal ligament) → profunda femoris (thigh muscles) + superficial femoral → popliteal → anterior tibial, posterior tibial, peroneal.

6. Management

  • Goals: ↓ MACE (MI, stroke, CV death) and ↓ MALE (major amputation, serious limb events); prolong survival, relieve symptoms, save the limb, improve quality of life. Every plan treats both the systemic risk and the limb.
  • Treatment map: smoking cessation (very important) · aggressive control of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia · diet, weight, exercise · antiplatelet · statin for all PAD — even with normal cholesterol · supervised exercise · revascularization for selected patients only (CLTI or refractory claudication).
  • Supervised exercise: ≥ 3 times/week, ~30 min per session — walk until claudication, continue into tolerable pain, rest ~3–4 min, repeat. Builds collaterals, muscle conditioning and walking efficiency.
  • Calf claudication relieved by rest, ABI 0.60/0.65 → best medical therapy and supervised exercise first. 442 ×5
Added explanationBuerger's disease (thromboangiitis obliterans): young male heavy smokers, distal small/medium arteries (digital ischaemia, rest pain, ulcers, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis). Complete smoking cessation is the only treatment that halts it and prevents amputation.
  • What decreases mortality/progression in Buerger's disease → smoking cessation. 439

Revascularization

  • Revascularize when: CLTI — rest pain, ulcers or tissue loss — with a salvageable limb, or lifestyle-limiting claudication despite medical therapy and structured exercise.
  • Avoid early intervention for uncomplicated claudication: many improve conservatively; repairs have limited durability; continued smoking worsens results.
Endovascular (angioplasty ± stent)Surgical bypass
Best forShort/focal lesionsLong/complex lesions, unfavourable anatomy, failed endovascular
Invasiveness / riskLowerHigher — more incisions, more perioperative risk
RecoveryFasterSlower
DurabilityOften lower — restenosis, repeat proceduresOften higher, especially with autologous vein
  • Angioplasty: guidewire across the lesion → balloon compresses the plaque (risk of recoil/re-narrowing) → stent holds the lumen. Bypass: from a patent artery above the block to a suitable artery below — autologous vein or prosthetic graft.
  • Bypass rather than conservative management → rest pain with gangrene of the toes (CLTI) — not claudication > 100 m, not a well-perfused or neuropathic ulcer. 439 ×6
  • Surgical rather than conservative → rest pain with gangrene of the toe (fragmentary recall). 427
  • Diabetic with a 1 × 2 cm forefoot ulcer and pain → keyed wound care and revascularization (both accepted); besides wound care, the most important step → revascularization. 439 ×5 439

7. Irreversible ischaemia & amputation

  • Late presentation with extensive necrosis — never reperfuse a dead limb (reperfusion injury):
Washed out of necrotic tissueSystemic effect
Potassium + acids/lactateHyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis → arrhythmias
MyoglobinAcute kidney injury
Toxic metabolitesARDS, systemic instability
  • Unsalvageable limb → major amputation (below- or above-knee by tissue viability). Limited tissue loss (one gangrenous toe) → minor amputation/debridement + revascularization.

Mastery checklist (notes)

  • PAD = marker of systemic atherosclerosis — MI/stroke/CV death are commoner than amputation.
  • Most PAD is asymptomatic.
  • Vascular claudication: reproducible, relieved by stopping; neurogenic: posture-dependent, needs sitting/flexion.
  • Buttock → aortoiliac; thigh → external iliac/proximal femoral; calf → distal disease.
  • CLTI = rest pain and/or tissue loss → revascularize a salvageable limb.
  • ABI = higher ankle ÷ higher brachial for each leg; ≤ 0.9 = PAD; > 1.4 = calcified → toe pressure/TBI.
  • Duplex cheap but operator-dependent; CTA/MRA for planning; catheter angiography when intervening.
  • Everyone: stop smoking, supervised exercise, statin (even normal cholesterol), antiplatelet, control DM/BP/lipids.
  • Endovascular = less invasive, less durable (short lesions); bypass = more durable (long lesions, autologous vein).
  • Never reperfuse a dead limb — amputate.
